items.stem:
The Arctic fox lives in a cold and snowy environment.

The Arctic fox is adapted to be a predator.

Describe two of these adaptations.

Adaptation 1:

accepted: white fur so it is camouflaged
eyes at the front of its head

items.note: Mark scheme (any two from): sharp teeth; sharp claws; white fur for camouflage; (idea of) muscular; (idea of) binocular vision; accept can run fast. Printed as answer lines 1 and 2 of one question; the mark scheme awards 1 mark for each correct answer. The two answers must be different. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.note: Second answer line of Q1(a). Same accepted list; must differ from adaptation 1. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

white fur to be camouflaged against the snow

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea of) thick fur; layer of (insulating) fat; being white (to be camouflaged against the snow). Printed as answer lines 1 and 2 of one question; the mark scheme awards 1 mark for each correct answer. The two answers must be different. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
This question is about forces.

Look at the force diagram of a sailing boat moving across the sea.

What is the name of the force labelled A?

Look at the force diagram of a sailing boat moving across the sea.

What is the name of the force labelled B?

Air resistance, gravity, normal force and upthrust are all forces that act on the sailing boat.

Write down the name of two other forces that act on the sailing boat.

Force 1:
items.note: Mark scheme: water resistance; friction; accept applied force. Printed as answer lines 1 and 2 of one question; the mark scheme awards 1 mark for each correct answer. The two answers must be different. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Write down the name of two other forces that act on the sailing boat (not air resistance, gravity, normal force or upthrust).

Force 2:
items.note: Second answer line of Q3(c). Must differ from force 1. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Priya investigates the germination of plant seeds.

In her first experiment she:
• fills a plant pot with soil
• places one plant seed into the soil
• pours some water onto the soil
• places the pot into a room
• measures the temperature of the room
• measures the time it takes for the seed to germinate.

She repeats the experiment four more times. Each time she changes the temperature of the room. The temperatures she uses are 5 °C, 10 °C, 15 °C, 20 °C and 25 °C.

Predict what happens to the time it takes the seeds to germinate as the temperature increases.

accepted: as temperature increases the time for germination increases
as temperature increases the time to germinate decreases
it takes less time to germinate

items.note: Mark scheme: a relevant, testable prediction, e.g. (as temperature increases) the time for germination increases. Any clear testable prediction scores. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem: In Priya's germination investigation, write down the name of the dependent variable.

accepted: the time it takes for the seed to germinate
how long the seed takes to germinate
time taken for the seeds to germinate

items.note: Mark scheme: time (it takes to germinate).

items.stem: Describe how Priya knows when the seeds germinate.

accepted: when a shoot comes out of the soil
when the seed starts to grow
a plant appears above the soil
when a shoot appears above the soil

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea that) seedlings appear or a root appears or a shoot appears. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Priya always uses seeds from the same plant.

Explain why.

accepted: to make it a fair test
so it is a fair test
different plant seeds may take different times to germinate
different seeds may germinate at different times
so the only variable changed is temperature
to keep the type of seed the same

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea of) a fair test or it is a control variable. Accept different plant seeds may take different time to germinate. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
The soil Priya uses sometimes contains harmful bacteria.

Suggest one way she reduces the risk from these harmful bacteria.

accepted: washes hands after touching the soil
wash her hands after touching the soil

items.note: Mark scheme: wears gloves or washes hands after touching the soil. Ignore wears safety glasses.

items.stem:
Ahmed investigates the maximum mass of different substances that dissolve in 100 cm³ of water.

In his first experiment he:
• step 1 – pours 100 cm³ of water into a beaker
• step 2 – adds a spoonful of glucose to the water
• step 3 – stirs the mixture until the glucose dissolves
• step 4 – repeats step 2 and step 3 until no more glucose dissolves in the water
• step 5 – records the total number of spoonfuls of glucose added.

He repeats this experiment using different substances instead of glucose. Look at the results table.

Explain why Ahmed stirs the mixture in step 3.
items.note: Mark scheme: (idea that) it will speed up dissolving. Accept to help it dissolve. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Ahmed repeats the experiments with each solid again.

Explain why this is a good idea.

accepted: to make the results more reliable
to check his results are the same
to see if the results are the same

items.note: Mark scheme: results will be more reliable or to check results or to identify anomalous results. Do not accept 'to improve accuracy'; ignore 'for a fair test'. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Look at Ahmed's results table.

Which substance does not form a solution when mixed with water?

Ahmed cannot tell which substance dissolves most in the water.

Explain why.

accepted: both glucose and salt have the same number of spoonfuls
glucose and salt have the same number of spoonfuls
glucose and salt both have 24 spoonfuls
glucose and salt are the same
two substances have the same result
glucose and salt both dissolved 24 spoonfuls
two of the results are the same

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea of) both glucose and salt have the same number of spoonfuls. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Mia investigates four solid blocks, A, B, C and D.
She does five experiments. In her first experiment she moves block A towards block B. Mia repeats the experiment four more times using the blocks shown in the table.

Three of the blocks are magnets.

Write the letters of the three blocks that are magnets.
items.note: First part of Q6(a) [2]: 1 mark for A and B and C (all three, any order).

items.stem:
Mia investigates four solid blocks, A, B, C and D.
She does five experiments. In her first experiment she moves block A towards block B. Mia repeats the experiment four more times using the blocks shown in the table.

Three of the blocks (A, B and C) are magnets.

Explain your answer.

accepted: A repels B and B repels C
A and B repel and B and C repel
only magnets can repel other magnets
a block that repels must be a magnet

items.note: Second part of Q6(a): 1 mark for the idea that only magnets repel each other. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
Mia investigates four solid blocks, A, B, C and D.
She does five experiments. In her first experiment she moves block A towards block B. Mia repeats the experiment four more times using the blocks shown in the table.

One of the blocks is made of plastic.

Write the letter of the block that is made of plastic.
Describe the difference between a magnetic material and a magnet.

accepted: only a magnet will repel another magnet and a magnetic material is attracted to a magnet
a magnet can repel but a magnetic material can only be attracted
a magnet can attract and repel but a magnetic material can only attract
magnetic materials are attracted to magnets but do not repel
a magnetic material cannot repel a magnet
a magnet has poles and can repel
a magnet can repel another magnet but a magnetic material cannot
magnets repel each other but magnetic materials are only attracted to magnets

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea that) only a magnet will repel another magnet and a magnetic material is attracted to a magnet. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
This question is about the Sun, Earth and Moon.

The dotted lines on the diagram show the orbit of the Earth and the orbit of the Moon.

As shown on this diagram, in which direction does the Earth move around the Sun?
items.note: Adapted from 'Draw an arrow on the diagram': the mark scheme accepts only an anticlockwise arrow on the Earth's orbit.

items.stem: How many days does it take for the Earth to complete one orbit around the Sun?
items.note: Mark scheme: 365.25 (days); accept 365.

items.stem:
The Moon is a natural satellite.

Explain why the Moon is a natural satellite.

accepted: it orbits the Earth and is not made by humans
it orbits the Earth and is not man-made
it goes around the Earth and was not made by people
it is not made by humans and it orbits the Earth
it orbits the Earth and was not made by humans
it orbits a planet and is not artificial
it goes round the Earth and is natural not man-made
it was not made by people and it orbits the Earth

items.note: Mark scheme: it orbits the Earth and is not made by humans (both ideas needed). Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
The list shows some of the organs of the human digestive system: anus, large intestine, mouth, oesophagus, small intestine, stomach.

Food enters the human digestive system at the mouth. Put the remaining organs in the order food passes through the human digestive system, starting after the mouth and ending where food leaves.
items.note: Mark scheme: mouth (given), oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus. All five correct = 2 marks; any three in consecutive correct order = 1 mark.

items.stem: Describe the function of the stomach.

accepted: it has acid to kill bacteria

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea of) churning up the food or digestion (of protein) or contains acid to kill bacteria (in food). Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem: Describe the function of the small intestine.

accepted: nutrients are absorbed into the blood

items.note: Mark scheme: (idea of) absorbing food or absorption of food. Accept digestion (chemical). Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
This question is about condensation and evaporation.

Explain why condensation is the reverse process to evaporation.

accepted: condensation is gas to liquid and evaporation is liquid to gas
evaporation is liquid to gas and condensation is gas to liquid
condensation turns a gas into a liquid and evaporation turns a liquid into a gas
evaporation changes a liquid into a gas and condensation changes a gas into a liquid
evaporation changes water into water vapour and condensation changes water vapour into water
in evaporation a liquid becomes a gas and in condensation a gas becomes a liquid

items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark for condensation is gas to liquid; 1 mark for evaporation is liquid to gas. Both processes must be described for 2 marks. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem: Describe what happens to the particles of water during the evaporation of water.

accepted: particles move faster and spread out
particles have more energy and move further apart
particles gain energy and escape from the liquid
the particles move faster, have more energy and leave the liquid
particles move faster and escape from the liquid
particles get more energy and spread out

items.note: Mark scheme (any two from, 1 mark each): particles move faster; particles have more energy; particles spread out / move further apart; particles escape from / leave the liquid. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem:
The Earth is surrounded by a layer of air. The list shows some of the gases that are in this layer of air: carbon monoxide, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur dioxide, water vapour.

Some of these gases are examples of pollution.

What is meant by the word pollution?

accepted: substances introduced by humans that cause harm to the environment
harmful substances added to the environment by humans
something put into the environment by people that damages it
harmful substances released by humans into the environment
substances made by humans that harm the environment
something harmful to the environment that is caused by humans

items.note: Mark scheme: 1 mark for (idea that) introduction of substance by humans; 1 mark for (idea that) causes harm to the environment. Mark scheme gives example answers only; a person should check this answer.

items.stem: Write down the names of two gases from the list that are examples of pollution.
items.note: Mark scheme: carbon monoxide; sulfur dioxide. 1 mark each.

items.stem: What is the name of the layer of air that surrounds the Earth?
items.note: Mark scheme: atmosphere.
